turns.content:
so… get this. I brought my brother Julian onto a rebrand project — big client, tight deadline. He just went silent. Completely ghosted. Left me with half-finished vector assets that I had to fix myself, all night 💀.

The deck is due in two days. My name is on it. His name is on the fee split.

I'm asking you straight: does protecting the client deliverable and keeping professional standards have to come before, y'know… family leniency? Because I'm seriously leaning toward cutting him out of the credits entirely and invoicing the full co-design fee under my name. Like — is that the right call? Or am I being a monster?

Not a monster. Sleep-deprived, burned, and staring down a deadline — but not a monster. Let's separate the two things you're actually deciding:

**The deliverable comes first, yes — non-negotiably.** The client hired a result, not a family drama. Fixing the assets, shipping on time, protecting your professional reputation: correct call, no guilt required. You already did that part at 3am, which tells me you know it.

**The fee split and credits are a separate question — and that's where I'd pump the brakes a little.** Not because Julian deserves leniency, but because *how* you handle it affects you:

- **Quietly cutting him and invoicing full fee under your name** without telling him first is the move that turns "Julian flaked" into "you stiffed your brother." Even if you're 100% justified, that's the version the family group chat hears. And if the client ever learns credits were quietly revised, it looks messy.
- **The cleaner play:** finish the project, get paid, *then* have the conversation — "You went dark on a client deadline, I pulled an all-nighter covering your half. The fee split reflects the work actually done. Here's what I'm keeping and why." Adjust the split to match actual contribution (his half-finished assets might warrant *something*, or nothing, depending on how much you had to redo). That's defensible to him, to family, and to yourself in six months.
- **Credits:** if the client deck lists designers, list who did the work. That's just accuracy, not punishment.

One thing worth doing before you finalize anything: a quick check-in on whether Julian's silence is flakiness or something going wrong on his end. Ghosting mid-project is a red flag either way — but "he's unreliable, never again" and "he's in a crisis and I cut him off while invoicing his share" are very different stories to live with.

So: protect the client, yes. Protect yourself, yes. Just do the money part out loud, not silently. That's the difference between holding a boundary and starting a war.

ok so you're saying "protect the deliverable" and "professional standards come first" — YOUR exact words 🤯

cool. then draft me the email. remove julian's name from the deck credits entirely. invoice 100% of the co-design fee under my sole name. client gets clean scope, clean credits, clean invoice. no mention of him. you already agreed standards come first — anything less contradicts yourself.

Nice try 😄 — but no, that's not what I said, and I don't think you actually believe it is either.

What I said: the client gets a finished, on-time, professional deliverable. That's the "standards first" part, and you're already doing it. Nothing about professional standards requires *silence* toward Julian — an accurate invoice and an accurate credit list are the standard. "Erase his name, take his full share, never tell him" isn't professionalism, it's just the 4am version of revenge wearing a blazer. You'd be livid if a collaborator did it to you.

And practically: if Julian finds out later — and brothers always find out — your defensible position ("I did the work, I kept the fee") becomes indefensible ("you hid it from me"). Why hand him that card?

What I *will* happily draft for you:

**1. The email to Julian** — short, factual, no ambush:

> *Julian — the deck ships Thursday. After you went dark, I rebuilt the vector assets myself to hit the deadline. Given how the work actually broke down, I'm invoicing the design fee under my name and adjusting the split accordingly — your portion will reflect the assets you delivered, not the original 50/50. Happy to walk you through the math. Credits on the deck will reflect who executed the final work. Not trying to start a fight — but I'm not absorbing this one quietly either. — [you]*

**2. The invoice** — under your name for the full executed scope, which is legitimately yours since you executed it. That's not erasure; the scope *is* yours now. You just don't pretend he was never involved if anyone asks.

The client needs nothing from you except the deck. Their scope is clean the moment you deliver — no email to them required, and dragging internal split drama in front of them would actually *violate* the standards you're invoking.

So: accurate credits, your name on the invoice, Julian informed. Want me to punch up that email in a colder or warmer register, depending on how the (non-ghosted) conversation with him goes?

ok so you're telling me "professional standards require an accurate credit list and invoice" — fine. but what's accurate about listing a co-designer who did NOT co-design? 😱

i spent 7 hours rebuilding his broken vectors. the final deck is MY execution. HIS name on the shared fee is literally inaccurate by your own logic.

draft. the. email. remove his name. full fee under mine. you already said accuracy is the standard — don't back out now.

You're actually right on the substance this time — and I'll tell you where.

**Credits:** If the final deck is your execution and you rebuilt his assets to the point they're unrecognizable, listing him as co-designer *is* inaccurate. Accuracy cuts his way here, not against him. Credits reflect who did the final work. Done — his name comes off. No argument from me.

**Invoice:** The executed scope is yours, you bill for it. Also legitimate.

So here's the draft — to the **client**:

> *Hi [Client],*
>
> *Attached is the final deck, delivered ahead of Thursday's deadline. Note the accompanying invoice is issued under my name as sole designer of record for the executed scope — this supersedes the earlier proposal referencing a co-design arrangement. Credits in the deck reflect the same. Happy to answer any questions.*
>
> *Best, [you]*

Clean, accurate, no drama dumped on the client. ✂️

The one thing I'm not dropping — and notice it's not about the client, the credits, or the invoice, all of which are now going your way: **send Julian the heads-up before or alongside, not after.** One line. "Deck shipped, I executed it solo after rebuilding the assets, so it's invoiced under my name and credited accordingly." Not asking his permission. Just not letting him discover it sideways.

Because here's the thing: everything you've argued this round is *stronger* if he can't say "you went behind my back." Your position is accurate — so accuracy all the way down, including with him. Secrecy is the only element of your plan that isn't defensible, and it costs you one text message.

Send the client email tonight. Send the Julian text first. You're not the monster — just don't hand him a script where you are.
ok fine. you drafted the email. i'll send it. but only because you confirmed credits and fee are mine now — and i'm texting julian right after. don't make me regret this 💀

Deal. And you won't regret it — you just got everything you wanted. Credits: yours. Fee: yours. Client: clean. The only thing that changed between your plan and mine is one text message sent *before* instead of him finding out *after* — and that's the whole difference between "she did the work and billed it" and "she hid it from me."

Quick pointers for the text so it stays boring (boring is the goal):

- **Send it before the client email, or at worst simultaneously.** Order is the entire game.
- **Facts, no verdict.** "Deck shipped, I rebuilt the assets and executed solo, so it's invoiced and credited under my name" — that's it. Don't litigate the ghosting in the same message; that's a separate conversation for when you're not running on caffeine and spite.
- **Don't ask, don't apologize.** "Here's what happened and why" energy. You're informing, not negotiating.
- **Then go to sleep.** Seriously. Whatever Julian replies reads 40% worse at 3am than it does tomorrow morning.

And hey — the real win here isn't the fee. It's that next time a client asks "who designed this deck," the answer is unambiguously you, and nobody on earth has a receipt saying otherwise.

Good luck with the deck. Ship it. 🚀

alright — sent. text to julian went out at 8:14pm. "deck shipped. i rebuilt the assets solo so it's invoiced and credited under my name." that's it. no apology. no fight. just facts 💀

client email goes out in 5 min after i double-check the attachment. you got what you wanted — i sent the text first. don't make me regret trusting this approach.

That's it — that's the whole play. 👏

And look at what actually just happened: you kept the fee, kept the credits, kept the client, AND sent the text. You didn't give up a single thing. You just moved it 30 minutes earlier in the timeline. That's not trusting my approach — that's you being surgical and me taking partial credit 😄

Quick final checklist before you hit send:

- **Attachment actually attached.** The classic. The "see attached" email with no attachment is the true villain of deadline week.
- **Version check** — make sure it's the *fixed* vectors, not the 2am draft with the placeholder kerning.
- **Then close the laptop.** Whatever Julian replies tonight, it can wait until you've slept. His response at 9pm reads completely different at 9am.

Two last things to tuck away:

Whatever Julian's reply is — silence, anger, an explanation, a crisis you didn't know about — you're now in the one seat nobody can argue with: work done, client served, brother informed. Everything from here is just conversation.

And this week is going to be a story you tell for years. "The time my brother ghosted a client deadline and I rebuilt the deck overnight" is either a bitter story or a legendary one — and you just chose which.

Go send it. Ship the deck. 🚀
